abstract: Genetic responses to forest management may vary substantially among saproxylic beetles because species differ in habitat requirements, dispersal and ecological specialization. Here, we evaluated whether microhaplotypes reconstructed from Double Digest Restriction-site Associated DNA sequencing (ddRADseq) loci provide additional locus-level genetic information and reveal species-specific associations with forest protection, management and habitat characteristics across 12 saproxylic beetle species sampled in eight forest complexes in Poland. Phased combinations of linked Single Nucleotide Polymorphism (SNPs) within RAD loci were analysed as multi-allelic microhaplotypes. Observed microhaplotype diversity was compared with analytical expectations under linkage equilibrium to assess how diversity differed from that expected if constituent SNP positions were independent. Observed microhaplotype diversity was consistently lower than expected under linkage equilibrium across all 12 species, with the magnitude of the difference varying among species. Patterns of population differentiation inferred from SNP-based FST and microhaplotype-based {Phi}ST were significantly concordant in all species, although the strength of correspondence varied considerably among taxa. Individual microhaplotype homozygosity (FHAP) showed heterogeneous associations with site protection and management categories, with no consistent directional response across species. Sensitivity analyses restricted to the NE Poland detected no significant management associations after correction for multiple testing. Associations between site-level microhaplotype diversity and habitat characteristics also varied among species. Species traits showed suggestive associations with management-related changes in FHAP, although none remained statistically significant after correction for multiple-testing. Overall, microhaplotypes retain linked within-locus genetic variation and broadly recover SNP-based patterns of population differentiation, while associations between forest context and genetic variation remain strongly species-dependent.
